seo.title: Student Budget: Manage Money on a Small Income
seo.description: A simple student budget guide: work out your real income, plan for term fees and books, cut everyday costs and save a little, even on a small allowance.

h1: Student budget: how to manage money on a small income
summary: Living on a grant, an allowance or a part-time job? A simple student budget helps your money last until the next payment and keeps you out of debt.
intro_html:
Being a student often means living on very little. Your money might come from family, a scholarship, a government grant or loan, a part-time job, or a mix of all of these. It may arrive once a month, once a term or whenever someone can send it. And it has to stretch across rent, food, travel, books and a social life.

A student budget does not have to be complicated. It is simply a plan for how your money will last until the next payment arrives. This guide shows you how to build one in a few simple steps, with tips that work whether you study in Lahore, Delhi, London, Dubai, Riyadh, Madrid, Mexico City or anywhere else.

sections.h2: Work out what really comes in
sections.body_html:
Start by listing every source of money and when it arrives:

  • Money from parents or relatives
  • Scholarships, bursaries or grants
  • Student loans paid to you for living costs
  • Wages from a part-time or holiday job
  • Any regular gifts or other income

Be honest about what is reliable. A parent's monthly transfer you can count on is different from a few shifts you might get at a café. Build your budget on the money you are sure of, and treat anything extra as a bonus for savings or treats.

If your money arrives once a term

Many grants and loans are paid in large lumps at the start of each term. That feels like a lot on day one, but it has to last for months. Divide the amount by the number of weeks or months until the next payment. That figure is your real weekly or monthly budget. Some students move the lump sum into a separate account and transfer themselves a fixed amount each week, like a mini salary.

sections.h2: List your costs, including the ones that come once a year
sections.body_html:
Next, write down what you spend. Split it into three groups.

Fixed monthly costs

Rent or hostel fees, your share of bills, phone plan, internet and travel passes. These are the first things to cover.

Everyday costs

Food, snacks, coffee, eating out, laundry, toiletries and going out with friends. These change from week to week, and they are where most of your savings can come from.

Term and yearly costs

Tuition or exam fees, textbooks, lab kits, uniforms, a laptop, travel home for holidays and festivals, and gifts. These are easy to forget because they don't happen every month. Add them up, divide by the number of months in the academic year, and set that amount aside each month so they never catch you by surprise.

If you are not sure what you spend on everyday things, track every purchase for two or three weeks. Most students are surprised by at least one category.

Once you know your income and your costs, put them together:

  1. Cover the essentials first: housing, bills, travel to classes and basic food.
  2. Set aside money for term costs such as books and fees.
  3. Save a small amount, even a very small one, for emergencies.
  4. Decide what is left for fun and stick to it.

A well-known starting point is the 50/30/20 split: about half for needs, about 30% for wants and about 20% for savings. On a student income, needs often take up much more than half, and that is normal. Use it as a rough guide rather than a target. Our 50/30/20 rule guide explains how to adapt it.

You can also put your numbers into the budget calculator. It shows how much of your money goes to each area and how much is left. Everything stays on your own device.

sections.h2: Everyday ways to make your money go further
sections.body_html:
Food

  • Cook in batches and share meals with flatmates or hostel friends. Cooking together is usually cheaper and more fun.
  • Plan meals for the week and shop with a list.
  • Take lunch and a water bottle to campus instead of buying them every day.
  • Look for markets and reduced-price items near closing time.

Books and study materials

  • Use the library first, including e-books and online journals your institution provides.
  • Buy second-hand books from older students, or share copies with classmates.
  • Sell your books at the end of the year.

Travel

  • Ask whether your city or transport provider offers a student pass or discount.
  • Walk or cycle short distances when it is safe.
  • Book long trips home early, when fares are often lower.

Phone and subscriptions

  • Choose a phone plan that matches what you actually use.
  • Check for student prices on music, video and software, and share family plans where the rules allow.
  • Cancel subscriptions you rarely use. Our subscription audit guide shows how to find them.

Student discounts

Many shops, cinemas, transport companies and software providers offer student discounts. Always carry your student card and ask. Even small discounts add up across a year.

Students are often offered credit: overdrafts, credit cards, "buy now, pay later" plans and instalment deals on phones and laptops. Some of these can be useful, but borrowing for everyday spending can build up quickly and follow you after you graduate.

  • Read the terms carefully, especially what happens if you pay late or when an interest-free period ends.
  • If you use a credit card, try to pay the full balance each month.
  • Avoid borrowing to pay for nights out, takeaways or other short-lived treats.
  • If you are struggling, speak to your college or university's student support or finance office. Many have hardship funds or can point you to free money advice.

Student loans for tuition and living costs are a separate matter. The rules for repaying them vary a lot from country to country, so check the official information from the body that provides your loan.

Your student budget will change every term as timetables, housing and jobs change. Take ten minutes each week, perhaps on the same day your money arrives, to look at what you have spent and what is left.

If you go over in one area, take a little from another rather than giving up. If your income is irregular, for example from shift work, our guide on saving money on an irregular income has ideas for smoothing out the ups and downs. The skills you build now will help you a lot when your first full salary arrives.

faq.q: How much money does a student need per month?
faq.a: It depends heavily on the country, the city and whether you live at home, in a hostel or in shared housing. The best way to find your number is to add up your own fixed costs and track your everyday spending for a few weeks.

faq.q: Should students try to save money?
faq.a: If you can, yes, even a small amount. A little emergency money can stop a broken phone or an unexpected fee from turning into debt.

faq.q: Is it worth getting a part-time job while studying?
faq.a: A part-time job can ease money pressure and build experience, but it should not harm your studies. Many universities and student visa rules limit working hours, so check what applies to you.

faq.q: What is the easiest way to stick to a student budget?
faq.a: Pay yourself a fixed weekly amount from your main account into a spending account or wallet, and only spend from that. When it runs out, you know to slow down until next week.
